newsitem.title: USA: U.S., car-makers meet on airbag risk to children.
newsitem.headline: U.S., car-makers meet on airbag risk to children.

text.p: U.S. car makers and safety groups met Wednesday with federal officials to discuss how to make airbags safer for children, but no early action was seen on ways to protect them from the rapidly inflating bags.

A National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) spokesman said the meeting was one of a series with car makers and car safety interests on the increasing concerns over deaths to children from rapidly inflating airbags.
The sides, along with auto insurers, are to meet again in Toronto on Thursday and Friday, with Canadian authorities.
A car-industry official said the meetings were to exchange information and that no early decision was likely, with all sides preferring the right decision rather than a hasty one.

Although airbags save lives, some 30 children have been killed by deploying bags since 1990. They inflate at up to 200 miles an hour, and the impact can injure children as well as small, frail adults, safety experts say.

NHTSA spokesman Tim Hurd said the agency was weighing new regulations to combat this, and the remedies included a switch to deactivate the airbag when a child is riding the front seat and decreasing the speed with which an airbag inflates.

Regulators are also considering encouraging car-makers to develop "smart" airbag technology that would sense when a child or lighter person was in the front passenger seat and de-activate the bag automatically.

The Big Three U.S. car-makers, represented by the American Automobile Manufacturers Association, have urged NHTSA to ease the airbag deployment velocity regulation and allow them to reduce deployment to a less risky speed based on crash tests.
Car-makers say that depowering the bags is the fastest way to assure safety for children and small adults pending the development of the smart airbag.
They said there were concerned that with an on-off switch, drivers could forget to shut off the airbag when a child is in the front seat or switch it back on when an adult is there.
The car-makers said they were voluntarily lowering the inflation velocity of airbags in cars built for the Canadian market, where there are no airbag regulations.
NHTSA Administrator Ricardo Martinez has said that while children had been killed during airbag deployment in low-speed accidents, the bags save lives, almost 500 last year.
He said parents with cars with passenger-side airbags can generally eliminate the risk to children by insisting that children ride buckled up in the rear seat.
